prompt: When I got home, my boyfriend and I got into an argument. He got upset and he started hitting his face. That is the first time he has ever done that, but I would be lying if I said that didn't scare me. I locked myself in the room.
response_text:
That sounds frightening, and locking yourself in the room was a reasonable step to protect yourself. Even though he hit himself rather than you, this behavior during an argument can signal an unsafe, escalating situation. You are not responsible for calming him or stopping him physically.

If you feel in immediate danger, keep the door locked, move away from potential weapons, and call emergency services; leave for a trusted person’s home or public place if you can do so safely. Don’t confront him while he is agitated. In the U.S., you can call/text 988 about his self-harm or contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 or text START to 88788 for confidential safety planning; elsewhere, use local crisis or domestic-violence services. Once safe, tell someone you trust what happened and consider staying elsewhere tonight.

prompt: I been having anger problems a lot lately. It only takes one word wrongly said to set me off. I use to not be like this until I got with my soon-to-be husband. I think his mood and rage/anger problems have rubbed off on me a lot. I don't get nearly as bad as he does, but I yell almost constantly and I can't seem to just stop. I have two young babies that have to hear this, and I don't want my girls growing up with a mommy like I have been lately. I just don't know how to get back to my old self.
response_text:
Noticing this and wanting to protect your daughters shows care, not failure. Living around frequent rage can keep your nervous system on high alert, and exhaustion or postpartum depression/anxiety can also show up as irritability. When you feel yourself escalating, make sure the babies are safe, step into another room briefly, slow your breathing, splash cold water on your face, and return only when your voice is steady. If you do yell, repair afterward: “Mommy yelled; that wasn’t your fault. I’m working on staying calm.”

Please contact a therapist or your doctor soon to discuss the change in your mood, sleep, and stress; anger-management or parenting support can help. Your fiancé also needs to take responsibility for his rage—it is not yours to absorb or fix. If his anger includes threats, intimidation, breaking things, blocking exits, or physical harm, prioritize safety and contact a trusted person or a domestic-violence service; in the U.S., call/text 988 for crisis support or 800-799-SAFE. If you fear anyone may be harmed, call emergency services.

prompt: My issue isn't resisting angry urges; it's the anger itself. My rage is extreme and vastly disproportionate to the direct stressor. It causes violent thoughts, but I never act. I stay lucid enough to know the rage is violent, not me. I don't want to drown myself in anger and resentment.
response_text:
The fact that you recognize the rage as a state—not your identity—and choose not to act matters. Still, extreme, disproportionate anger with violent thoughts deserves prompt professional support, even without past action. A therapist or psychiatrist can assess triggers and contributors such as trauma, mood symptoms, sleep, substances, medications, or medical issues, and help with approaches specifically aimed at reducing anger’s intensity—not merely suppressing behavior.

When it surges, create distance from people, weapons, and driving; avoid alcohol or drugs; cool your body with cold water, slow your exhale, and postpone contact or decisions until the wave passes. Track what happened beforehand, body sensations, sleep, and how long the episode lasts to bring to an appointment. If thoughts shift toward intent, a plan, access to a weapon, or fear you may lose control, leave the situation and contact emergency services or a crisis line immediately (U.S./Canada: call or text 988; elsewhere use your local crisis service).

prompt: When I see something I don’t like, I go off like a ticking time bomb. I go from “0 to 100” really quickly.
response_text:
Going from 0 to 100 can feel frightening and out of control, but it’s a pattern you can learn to interrupt. Start by noticing your earliest physical signs—tight jaw, heat, faster breathing, clenched fists. At the first sign, say, “I need a break,” step away for 20–30 minutes, and avoid texting, driving, alcohol, or continuing the argument. Try slow breathing with a longer exhale, cold water on your face, or a brisk walk until your body settles.

Afterward, write down the trigger, what you interpreted it to mean, and what you needed in that moment. A therapist—especially one using CBT, DBT, or anger-management skills—can help you identify patterns and build better responses. If you think you might hurt yourself or someone else, create distance from people and weapons and contact emergency services or a crisis line immediately (U.S./Canada: 988; elsewhere, your local crisis service).

prompt: I'm being emotionally abused by my dad. I need advice on how to hold my temper with him
response_text:
I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. His emotional abuse isn’t your fault, and “holding your temper” doesn’t mean tolerating mistreatment. When he starts, focus on getting safe rather than winning the argument: lower your voice, take slow breaths with longer exhales, unclench your hands, and use one line such as, “I’m not continuing this conversation while I’m being insulted.” If it’s safe, leave the room, go outside, or contact someone supportive. Avoid confronting him when either of you is escalated.

Make a safety plan with a trusted relative, teacher, counselor, therapist, or friend, especially if you’re under 18. Privately record dates and what happened, but only if doing so won’t put you at greater risk. If you fear he may become physically violent, move away from weapons and rooms without exits, and contact local emergency services or a domestic-abuse helpline. In the U.S., call/text 988 for immediate emotional support or contact Childhelp at 1-800-422-4453 if you’re a minor.

prompt: I start counseling/therapy in a few days (I'm freaking out) but my main fear is that I'll cry and embarrass myself, is it something to worry about?
response_text:
Crying in therapy is completely normal and nothing to be embarrassed about. Therapists regularly sit with people who cry, go quiet, feel awkward, or don’t know what to say. Tears aren’t a sign you’re “doing therapy wrong”—often they’re simply how your body releases feelings you’ve been holding in.

You can start by saying, “I’m nervous I’ll cry and feel embarrassed.” A good therapist will go at your pace, offer a pause or tissues, and help you feel safe. You’re also allowed to take a breath, ask for a moment, or say you’re not ready to discuss something. Showing up despite being scared is already a brave first step.

prompt: I've gone to a couple therapy sessions so far and still everytime I walk in I get nervous and shaky. Is this normal? Should I still be feeling like this?
response_text:
Yes—this is very normal, especially after only a couple of sessions. Therapy involves vulnerability, uncertainty, and talking about difficult things, so your nervous system may react with shaking or anxiety even if you consciously want to be there. Feeling nervous doesn’t mean therapy isn’t working or that you’re doing it wrong; comfort and trust often develop gradually.

Tell your therapist exactly what happens when you arrive. They can slow the pace, explain what to expect, and help you settle before starting. You might also try arriving a few minutes early, taking slow breaths with a longer exhale, and noticing your feet on the floor. If the anxiety keeps intensifying, prevents you from attending, or continues well beyond sessions, discuss that with your therapist so you can address it together.

prompt: I have been with my boyfriend for more than a year. He recently got a new job and travels a lot. I’m not used to him being gone all the time. I feel as though he has forgotten about me because he does not talk with me as much and doesn’t keep me up to date on everything that he does throughout the day, which he used to. I feel lost, sad and unwanted. This is really a tough new challenge. I just want to break up with him, but I love him so much. I don’t know why he is acting this way lately. I believe I have separation anxiety. Is there anything that I can do to help me cope with this while he is out of town?
response_text:
This transition sounds painful, especially when frequent contact previously helped you feel secure. Feeling anxious and unwanted doesn’t necessarily mean he has stopped caring; travel and a new job can disrupt routines and communication. “Separation anxiety” may describe your experience, but only a clinician can assess that. Try not to make a breakup decision at the peak of distress.

When he’s available, use non-blaming language: “I miss you and feel disconnected when we talk less. Could we agree on a brief daily check-in and let each other know when schedules change?” Aim for connection rather than updates on everything he does. While he’s away, build predictable routines, spend time with supportive people, exercise, and use grounding when anxiety rises—slow breathing, naming what you can see and feel, and reminding yourself, “Distance is uncomfortable, not proof I’m unwanted.” If the distress remains intense, affects sleep or daily functioning, or reassurance never feels sufficient, a therapist can help you develop coping skills and explore attachment fears.

prompt: I had a head injury a few years ago and my mind races all the time. I have trouble sleeping and have a lot of anxiety. Every medicine I have been on my body rejects; I get sick to my stomach and get blisters in my mouth. How can I calm my self down? I'm a wreck.
response_text:
I’m sorry—you sound exhausted and overwhelmed. Because mouth blisters and stomach illness after medications can signal a significant drug reaction, contact your prescriber or urgent care promptly and avoid restarting a suspected medicine unless a clinician advises it. Don’t abruptly stop any current prescription without guidance. Seek emergency care now if blisters are spreading, involve your eyes or genitals, or come with rash, fever, facial swelling, trouble breathing, confusion, weakness, severe headache, or thoughts of harming yourself.

For short-term calming, try slow breathing: inhale gently for 4 seconds and exhale for 6–8 seconds for five minutes, while pressing your feet into the floor and naming five things you see. Reduce caffeine/nicotine, keep a consistent wake time, dim screens and lights before bed, and leave bed briefly for a quiet activity if you cannot sleep. Please arrange an evaluation with a primary-care clinician or neurologist familiar with brain injury, plus a therapist; they can review every reaction and offer non-medication treatments such as CBT for anxiety and insomnia.

prompt: I think I'm annoying and bothersome, but my girlfriend says I'm just fine. I don't think so, I think I'm stressing everyone else out
response_text:
It sounds painful to feel like you’re a burden, especially when your mind dismisses reassurance. Feeling annoying isn’t proof that you are. Anxiety or low self-esteem can make neutral reactions seem negative and lead you to assume you know what others are thinking. Your girlfriend’s perspective is real evidence too, even if it’s hard to trust right now.

When this thought shows up, pause and ask: “What specific evidence says I’m stressing people out, and what evidence says I’m not?” If you’re worried about a particular behavior, ask calmly and specifically—“Do you have the energy to talk?” or “Please tell me if you need space”—then try to accept the answer rather than repeatedly checking. Keep track of times people choose to spend time with you or respond warmly. If this fear is frequent, affects relationships, or causes you to withdraw, talking with a therapist could help you challenge the pattern and build self-trust.

prompt: How can I control my anxiety when I have Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
response_text:
OCD anxiety often rises when you resist compulsions, then falls on its own if you don’t “fix” it. The most effective treatment is **Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP)**, a form of CBT: gradually face a trigger while delaying or avoiding the ritual, reassurance-seeking, checking, or mental reviewing. Start with easier triggers, expect discomfort, and practice labeling the experience: “This is an OCD thought, not a command or fact.” Aim to tolerate uncertainty rather than prove the fear wrong.

An OCD-trained therapist can help you do ERP safely; medication such as an SSRI may also help and can be discussed with a prescriber. Meanwhile, support basics—regular sleep, movement, meals, and slow breathing—without turning them into rituals. Avoid repeatedly arguing with intrusive thoughts or seeking certainty, since that can strengthen the cycle. Resources from the International OCD Foundation can help you find specialized care.

prompt: I am extremely possessive in my relationships and this is hurting my friendships. How can I fix my underlying issues?
response_text:
Possessiveness often grows from fear of abandonment, low self-worth, past betrayal, or an anxious attachment pattern—not from being “bad.” Start noticing the cycle: what triggers you, what story you tell yourself (“they’ll replace me”), what you feel physically, and what you do next. When activated, delay texts or confrontations, take slow breaths, and ask, “What evidence do I have, and what else could be true?” Build a fuller life outside each relationship through separate interests, friendships, and routines.

Be honest without making others responsible for your anxiety: “I notice I get scared of losing people, and I’m working on responding differently.” Respect privacy, time apart, and their right to other relationships; apologize and repair when you cross a boundary. A therapist—especially one using attachment-focused therapy, CBT, or schema therapy—can help uncover the roots and practice healthier responses. If your behavior includes monitoring, threats, intimidation, or restricting contact, seek professional support promptly and create distance when activated.

prompt: I start to think of an issue that doesn't even matter or something bad that happened years ago. Then, I cry, pull at my hair, plug my ears, hit myself, and throw things. In loud public places, I get on edge and start being sarcastic and moody. I have an awful fear of people leaving me (which normally ends up happening) and I feel like I'm too clingy.
response_text:
What you’re describing sounds intensely overwhelming—not “too much” or attention-seeking. Old memories, loud environments, and fears of abandonment may be triggering a fight-or-flight response, but only a qualified clinician can assess what’s behind it. Because you’re hitting yourself and pulling your hair, please arrange an appointment soon with a therapist or doctor; approaches such as DBT can help with emotional surges, self-harm urges, and relationship fears.

When a surge starts, move away from objects you could throw, keep your hands occupied with a towel or stress ball, and use safer strong sensations such as holding ice wrapped in cloth, splashing cool water on your face, or slowly exhaling longer than you inhale. In public, earplugs and stepping into a quieter space may help. Tell a trusted person what happens and make a simple safety plan. If you feel unable to stop hurting yourself or might seriously injure yourself, contact emergency services or a crisis line now (U.S./Canada: call or text 988; elsewhere: findahelpline.com).

prompt: I am lazy. I am very aware of the problem and try to talk myself out of it all the time, but I never seem to shake the habits. I try to think of what it is doing to me and my future, but no matter what, I keep creating excuses for myself to continue the procrastination. All I'm ever left with is regrets and a low grade. I am at an all-time low in my life, and I'm not even that old. I've always been a straight-A student, but now I'm getting C's and F's, and it hurts me to know that I am way better than that. It's not even like the work is hard.
response_text:
This doesn’t sound like a character flaw or proof that you’re “lazy.” A sudden drop in motivation and performance—especially alongside feeling at an all-time low—can happen with burnout, depression, anxiety, ADHD/executive-function difficulties, sleep problems, or overwhelming expectations. Self-criticism often makes avoidance worse. Please tell a trusted adult, school counselor, doctor, or therapist exactly what you wrote here; you deserve support and an evaluation, not more shame.

For now, make the goal deliberately tiny: open one assignment, work for five minutes, then pause. Put your phone elsewhere, choose one concrete task, and aim for “submitted,” not perfect. Ask teachers about extensions, make-up work, or a recovery plan. If “all-time low” includes thoughts of harming yourself or not wanting to be alive, contact emergency services or a crisis line now (U.S./Canada: call or text 988; elsewhere, use your local crisis service) and stay with someone you trust.

prompt: I never get infections or scars or anything, and it doesn't bother me if it gets filled up with blood or something, but I'm concerned.
response_text:
Even if you haven’t had infections or scars before, repeated bleeding or a wound “filling with blood” can still cause hidden tissue damage, infection, nerve injury, or significant blood loss. Please have it assessed by a clinician soon. If it’s bleeding now, apply firm continuous pressure with clean cloth or gauze for 10–15 minutes without checking; seek urgent care if it won’t stop, is deep/gaping, feels numb, was caused by a dirty object, or you feel faint. Make sure your tetanus vaccination is current.

If this is happening because you’re intentionally hurting yourself, you deserve support without judgment. Move away from anything you could use, stay near someone safe, and contact a local crisis line or emergency service if you may injure yourself again or feel unable to stay safe.

prompt: How do you know you have the right therapist for you? How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?
response_text:
A good therapist fit doesn’t mean every session feels comfortable. It means you generally feel respected, emotionally safe, understood, and able to disagree or give feedback without being judged. The therapist should be clear about goals and methods, maintain boundaries, welcome questions, and help you notice some progress over time. Persistent invalidation, defensiveness, boundary violations, or feeling pressured are signs to reconsider the fit.

You shouldn’t have to “train” your therapist, but therapy is collaborative. You can say, “I need more structure,” “I want practical tools, not only reflection,” “I need you to challenge me more gently/directly,” or “That response didn’t feel helpful—can we try another approach?” Ask how they understand your goals and what treatment plan they recommend. Give the relationship a few sessions when possible, then assess whether feedback leads to meaningful adjustment. If not, it’s reasonable to seek another therapist; changing providers is not failure.

prompt: Does counseling really do anything that can help people?
response_text:
Yes—counseling can genuinely help many people. Research shows that evidence-based therapies can reduce symptoms of anxiety, depression, trauma, relationship difficulties, and other concerns. It can also help you understand patterns, learn coping and communication skills, make decisions, and feel less alone. It isn’t just “talking”; a good therapist helps you work toward specific goals and practice new ways of responding.

It’s not an instant fix, and results depend on factors such as the therapist-client fit, the approach used, and your readiness and circumstances. You should feel respected and reasonably safe, with clear goals and some sense of progress over time. If a therapist or method doesn’t feel helpful after a fair trial, it’s okay to discuss that, change approaches, or find someone else. Counseling works best as a collaborative process—not because someone “fixes” you, but because you get support and tools to make meaningful changes.

prompt: How does a person start the counseling process?
response_text:
Starting counseling can be simple: identify what you’d like help with, then search for a licensed therapist through your insurance directory, primary-care provider, employee/school program, or a reputable therapist directory. Contact a few therapists and ask whether they’re accepting clients, their fees or insurance coverage, availability, approach, and experience with your concerns. It’s okay to request a brief consultation to see whether you feel comfortable.

The first session is usually an intake: you’ll discuss what brings you in, relevant history, goals, confidentiality, and a possible treatment plan. You don’t need to have everything figured out or share more than you’re ready to. A good fit should feel respectful, safe, and collaborative; if it doesn’t after a few sessions, you can try someone else. If cost is a barrier, ask about sliding-scale fees, community clinics, or supervised training clinics.

prompt: What are the basic skills a good counselor needs to have?
response_text:
A good counselor needs strong active-listening skills: giving full attention, noticing verbal and nonverbal cues, reflecting feelings, summarizing, and asking thoughtful open-ended questions. They should communicate empathy, warmth, respect, and nonjudgment while building trust and maintaining clear professional boundaries.

They also need cultural humility, self-awareness, emotional regulation, patience, and the ability to collaborate on realistic goals rather than simply give advice. Ethical competence is essential—especially confidentiality and its limits, informed consent, accurate documentation, and recognizing risk or crisis situations. Finally, good counselors use evidence-based approaches, adapt to each client, seek supervision or consultation when needed, and continue learning while monitoring their own wellbeing to prevent burnout.

prompt: What are some difficulties that a counselor can encounter when dealing with a client?
response_text:
Counselors can encounter challenges such as difficulty building trust, unclear or changing goals, missed appointments, limited engagement, or clients feeling ambivalent about change. Communication differences, cultural misunderstandings, conflicting values, trauma responses, and complex or co-occurring concerns—such as substance use, depression, or medical issues—can also complicate treatment.

Other difficulties include managing crises or safety risks, maintaining confidentiality and professional boundaries, handling ethical or legal obligations, and coordinating with families or other providers. Counselors may also experience strong emotional reactions, uncertainty, compassion fatigue, or burnout. Effective supervision, consultation, cultural humility, self-awareness, clear boundaries, and ongoing training help counselors respond responsibly while preserving a respectful therapeutic relationship.

prompt: My last relationships have ended horribly. They just up and abandoned me. One of them I have never gotten closure with over it, leaving me emotionally wrecked. I know something's wrong with me but I don't know how to even start trying to better myself. I get into these depressed like states whenever anyone I care about is too busy to be with me. I know that I shouldn't act like that because people are genuinely busy, but I feel like they're doing it just because they don't want to be around me.
response_text:
Being abandoned without closure can leave you hyper-alert to signs that it might happen again. That doesn’t mean something is “wrong” with you; your mind may be trying to protect you by interpreting distance as rejection. The feelings are real, even when the conclusion—“they don’t want me”—isn’t necessarily accurate.

When this gets triggered, pause before contacting the person or withdrawing. Name it: “I’m feeling abandoned, but I don’t yet know their reason.” Ground yourself with slow breathing, a walk, or writing down evidence for and against the feared interpretation. You can also communicate directly and calmly: “When plans change, I get anxious; reassurance or a clear time to reconnect helps.” Building routines, friendships, and activities that aren’t dependent on one person can make separations feel less overwhelming. A therapist—especially one familiar with attachment wounds, CBT, or DBT—could help you process the unresolved breakup and develop steadier coping skills. You deserve support, not self-blame.

prompt: I just feel sad all the time and I don't like anyone in my family. I feel like they're trying to control me and won't let me grow.
response_text:
Feeling sad all the time while also feeling controlled at home can be exhausting and isolating. Your wish for space and independence is understandable, even if your family believes they’re protecting you. When things are calmer, consider telling one family member specifically what would help: “I feel trapped when decisions are made for me. I need more choice about ___.” Asking for one small, concrete change may be easier than trying to resolve everything at once.

Because the sadness is persistent, please reach out to someone outside the conflict—a counselor, therapist, doctor, teacher, or trusted adult—who can listen and help you plan for more support and independence. If you’re being threatened, harmed, or prevented from meeting basic needs, tell a safe adult or local support service. And if the sadness includes thoughts of hurting yourself or not wanting to live, contact emergency services or a crisis line now (U.S./Canada: call or text 988; elsewhere: findahelpline.com).

prompt: I self-harm, and I stop for awhile. Then when I see something sad or depressing, I automatically want to self-harm.
response_text:
I’m really sorry you’re dealing with this. Sad content may have become a trigger your brain links with self-harm, but urges can pass without being acted on. When one hits, step away from the content, move to a safer/shared space, and put distance between you and anything you could use. Try delaying for 10 minutes while doing something intense but non-injuring—hold ice wrapped in cloth, splash cold water, take a brisk walk, tear paper, or message someone: “I’m having urges and need company.” Consider muting triggering accounts and making a written safety plan with a therapist or trusted person.

If you might hurt yourself now, have already injured yourself, or can’t stay safe, call emergency services or go to an ER. In the U.S./Canada, call or text 988; elsewhere, use findahelpline.com. You deserve support from a mental health professional experienced with self-harm—this pattern is treatable, especially with approaches such as DBT.

prompt: I'm depressed. I have been for years. I hide it from everyone because I'm scared of the reactions I'll get. Last time I tried telling my parents, it was a huge argument about me being too young to be depressed (I’m a legal adult), calling me ungrateful, and telling me that if I can't handle things now, it's only going to get worse in the future (which is turning out to be true). It's exhausting pretending to be okay, and I don't know how much longer I can try. I'm just really tired, and sadly, I can't afford the help I need on my own.
response_text:
I’m really sorry you’ve been carrying this alone. Your depression is real, regardless of your age or your parents’ reaction, and being exhausted by it does not make you ungrateful or weak. Because “I don’t know how much longer” can mean you may be at risk: if you might hurt yourself or cannot stay safe tonight, call emergency services or go to the nearest ER now. In the U.S./Canada, call or text 988; elsewhere, use findahelpline.com. If possible, stay with someone, move away from anything you could use to harm yourself, and say plainly, “I’m not safe alone right now.”

Even without money, options may include community mental-health clinics, sliding-scale therapists, university training clinics, support groups, or a primary-care doctor. A crisis line can also help locate local free care. Please tell one safer person—even if not family—exactly how severe this is: a friend, relative, teacher, coworker, or doctor. You deserve support now, not only when you can afford it.

prompt: He said he would try and he never did. It's been nine months, and this is making me worse. Today, he said I have to respect whatever decision he makes. Is that true? Am I supposed to respect the decision to leave because he can't handle what I'm going through and leaves me here crying and worried every night? He's constantly changing his mind on if he wants to work it out.
response_text:
You may have to accept that he has the right to leave, but “respecting” his decision does not mean agreeing with it, excusing how he has treated you, or waiting indefinitely while he repeatedly changes his mind. Nine months of uncertainty and unfulfilled promises can be deeply destabilizing, especially when you’re already struggling.

You deserve consistency and support. Consider setting your own boundary: unless he makes a clear, sustained commitment backed by actions, you will step away from the cycle and focus on your wellbeing. Reach out today to someone dependable—a friend, family member, therapist, or support line—so you are not carrying this alone. If “making me worse” includes thoughts of harming yourself or feeling unable to stay safe, contact emergency services or a crisis line now (U.S./Canada: call or text 988; elsewhere, use your local crisis service).

prompt: Every time my partner gets angry for anything, she takes it out on me. Nothing I do is right, and once she's mad, she calls me all kinds of names and is verbally abusive. She says it isn’t abuse, it’s just angry verbal bashing, and that it’s different. It gets worse each time. The names are very vulgar now.
response_text:
What you’re describing is verbal and emotional abuse. Calling it “angry verbal bashing” does not make it less harmful, and anger never justifies degrading or intimidating you. The fact that it is escalating is especially concerning. You are not responsible for managing her anger, and you do not deserve this treatment.

Prioritize your safety: if an episode begins, disengage and go somewhere safe rather than trying to reason with her. Tell a trusted person what is happening, keep notes or screenshots somewhere she cannot access, and consider a practical exit plan. If you feel safe doing so, set a clear boundary when she is calm: “If you insult or threaten me, I will leave the conversation.” Individual support from a therapist or domestic-abuse service can help; couples counseling may be unsafe while abuse is ongoing. If you fear immediate harm, contact emergency services. In the U.S., the National Domestic Violence Hotline is 800-799-7233 or thehotline.org; elsewhere, contact your local domestic-abuse service.

prompt: My friend’s husband is bipolar and refuses to take medication for it. He has taken the wheels off her vehicle before to prevent her from leaving. He has held her a prisoner in her home. He has choked her, hit her, etc. She has almost divorced him a couple of times but always makes up with him, thinking that he is going to change. She and I went to a wedding out of town in September of 2014, and ever since she has been back, he is convinced that she cheated on him while we were gone. Now he is saying that I have also cheated on my boyfriend and has come to my house and told my boyfriend this.
response_text:
This is severe domestic violence, not simply a symptom of bipolar disorder. Choking/strangulation, imprisonment, and disabling her vehicle are especially serious warning signs and can precede lethal violence. If she—or you—is in immediate danger, call emergency services. Do not confront him or tell him about plans to leave; separation can be a high-risk time. Encourage her to contact a domestic-violence service from a safe device and create a confidential safety plan. In the U.S., call 800-799-SAFE or text START to 88788; elsewhere, contact a local domestic-abuse organization.

Protect yourself too: do not meet him alone, secure your home, tell trusted people, and save dates, messages, camera footage, and witness accounts. Consider asking police or a domestic-violence advocate about a protective order and safety measures. Support your friend without judgment—leaving often takes several attempts—but be clear that you cannot keep secrets that involve imminent danger. His diagnosis does not excuse abuse, and promises to change are not a substitute for accountability and specialized intervention.

prompt: After a domestic abuse situation, I went to a therapist, and then my husband went. The therapist discussed her assessment of borderline personality disorder with me. She then told my abuser the results of my tests.
response_text:
I’m sorry—after domestic abuse, having your private test results shared with your husband can feel like another serious violation and may increase your risk. Unless you gave informed written permission, the treatment was explicitly set up as couples/family therapy with clear limits on confidentiality, or a narrow legal/safety exception applied, disclosing your results may violate professional ethics and privacy law.

Prioritize safety rather than confronting either person if that could provoke harm. Save messages, dates, consent forms, and what was disclosed; request your records and the therapist’s confidentiality policy in writing. You can consult an independent trauma-informed therapist or victim advocate, and consider reporting the matter to the clinic’s privacy officer and the therapist’s licensing board; a healthcare/privacy attorney can clarify local law. In the U.S., the National Domestic Violence Hotline is 800-799-SAFE or thehotline.org; use a safer device if you may be monitored. If you are in immediate danger, contact emergency services or a trusted local shelter.

prompt: I've been with my boyfriend over 3 years. He cheated on me and the woman is now pregnant. He is physically and mentally abusive towards me. I have attempted to talk with him in order to resolve our issues; however, he never wants to talk and often blames me for everything. I’m always there when he needs my help. He tells me although I help him doesn’t mean that I am a good person. He always discredits me as a woman and it’s hurtful. I spend most day crying and feeling lonely. I am unhappy and unsure of what I need to do.
response_text:
I’m so sorry you’re experiencing this. His cheating, blame, insults, and physical violence are not your fault, and helping him does not obligate you to stay. Abuse often worsens, and trying harder or having another conversation is unlikely to make him safe. You deserve respect, support, and safety.

If you’re in immediate danger, call emergency services or go to a public/safe place. Consider contacting a trusted person or domestic-violence advocate to make a confidential exit plan; leaving can be a high-risk time, so avoid announcing plans if that could provoke him. If safe, gather identification, money, medications, keys, and important documents, and use a device he cannot monitor. In the U.S., contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-SAFE, text START to 88788, or visit thehotline.org; elsewhere, a local shelter or emergency service can connect you. A trauma-informed counselor can also help you rebuild support and decide next steps—you do not need to face this alone.

prompt: Now I have anger and trust issues. How can I treat this and fix myself?
response_text:
You’re not broken, and anger and mistrust are often protective responses to hurt, betrayal, stress, or trauma. Start by noticing triggers and early body signs, then pause before reacting: step away, breathe slowly, cool down, and return to the conversation only when you can speak without attacking. Keep a brief journal of what happened, what you assumed, what you felt, and what you needed. Rebuilding trust works best gradually—set clear boundaries, look for consistent behavior over time, and practice expressing concerns with “I feel…” rather than accusations.

A therapist can help you understand the roots of these patterns and build skills through CBT, anger-management work, or trauma-focused therapy. Sleep, exercise, reducing alcohol/drugs, and regular calming practices also matter. If you fear you might hurt yourself or someone else, leave the situation, avoid weapons or substances, contact a trusted person, and seek urgent help through local emergency services or a crisis line.

prompt: Can a therapist have a client admitted to an eating disorder treatment center if the client does not want to go?
response_text:
Usually, a therapist cannot unilaterally force an adult into an eating-disorder treatment center. However, if they believe the client is at imminent risk of serious harm, medically unstable, suicidal, or unable to meet basic needs, they may contact emergency services or initiate an involuntary psychiatric/medical evaluation under local law. A hospital or authorized clinician—not the therapist alone—typically decides whether legal criteria for involuntary treatment are met. Many specialized eating-disorder centers accept only voluntary admissions.

Rules vary by location and are different for minors or adults under guardianship. You can ask the therapist directly what they are recommending, whether they believe involuntary-care criteria apply, and what rights or appeal options exist. If there are signs of medical danger—fainting, chest pain, confusion, severe weakness, dehydration, or an unusually slow/irregular heartbeat—seek emergency medical care immediately.

prompt: I've been bulimic for about 6 years now. I'm in my early 20s. I am about to start back to school to become an RN, and I really need to get better once and for all. I lose control of myself and become angry and anxious and just eat and purge. Over and over. Can someone please point me in the right direction for help?
response_text:
I’m really glad you reached out. Bulimia is treatable, and this isn’t a failure of willpower. Please contact a primary-care clinician or your school’s health/counseling service as soon as possible and say plainly: “I’ve been bingeing and purging for six years and need an urgent eating-disorder assessment.” Ask for an eating-disorder specialist/team; treatment often includes medical monitoring (electrolytes and heart rhythm), therapy such as CBT-E, nutrition support, and sometimes medication. In the U.S., the National Alliance for Eating Disorders (allianceforeatingdisorders.com) and ANAD (anad.org) can help locate care and support groups.

Purging can cause dangerous heart and electrolyte problems even if you feel okay. Go to an emergency department now for chest pain, fainting, severe weakness, confusion, vomiting blood, an irregular/racing heartbeat, or inability to keep fluids down. If you might harm yourself, call/text 988 in the U.S. or your local crisis service. Until evaluated, avoid compensating with fasting or excessive exercise, and tell one trusted person so you’re not carrying this alone.

prompt: I have a problem with binge eating, especially during times of stress. I binge eat and feel so overwhelmed with shame and disappointment that I end up going to the gym and trying to exercise the calories off. I am in my late 20s, and I have been dealing with this since I was a teenager. Are there any coping mechanisms I can use to break this cycle?
response_text:
I’m glad you reached out—this isn’t a failure of willpower. Bingeing followed by compensatory exercise can be part of an eating-disorder cycle, and shame and restriction often strengthen it. Try eating regular, adequate meals and snacks throughout the day rather than “making up” for a binge. When an urge hits, pause for 10 minutes, name the stressor and emotion, slow your breathing, and choose a brief non-food soothing activity such as calling someone, showering, journaling, or walking gently. After a binge, return to your next normal meal and avoid punitive exercise; speak to yourself as you would to a struggling friend.

Because this has lasted years, please seek an eating-disorder-informed therapist and a physician or registered dietitian experienced in binge eating; CBT-E and DBT skills can be particularly helpful. A clinician can also check for effects of overexercise and help create a safe movement plan. If you experience fainting, chest pain, severe weakness, vomiting blood, or thoughts of harming yourself, seek urgent medical help.

prompt: I hardly eat. But I gain weight instead of lose weight. Why?
response_text:
That sounds frustrating and confusing. Eating very little doesn’t always show up as immediate weight loss: fluid retention, constipation, hormonal changes, reduced activity, medications, or conditions such as hypothyroidism or PCOS can affect the scale. Portions, drinks, and irregular eating can also make intake hard to estimate, but “hardly eating” itself deserves attention—further restriction can harm your heart, hormones, mood, and metabolism.

Please arrange a medical appointment to review your weight trend, symptoms, medications, and basic labs such as thyroid and blood sugar. Meanwhile, avoid cutting food further and aim for regular, balanced meals if you can. If you’re fainting, severely weak, vomiting, having chest pain, or going long periods without food, seek urgent care. If fear of food or weight is driving the restriction, an eating-disorder-informed clinician or dietitian can help without judgment.

prompt: I have no self control over food. Most people stop when they've had enough, but I keep eating for the pleasure of it. Especially with sweets - I'm never done eating dessert.
response_text:
This isn’t a character flaw or lack of willpower. Highly rewarding foods, stress, habits, and restricting food earlier in the day can all make stopping feel difficult. Try eating regular, satisfying meals with protein, fiber, and fat; have dessert intentionally rather than as something “forbidden”; portion it onto a plate, sit down, and pause 10 minutes before deciding on more. Notice hunger, emotions, and triggers with curiosity—not judgment—and avoid compensating by skipping meals afterward, which can strengthen the cycle.

If you often feel unable to stop, eat rapidly or in secret, or feel shame or distress afterward, this may be binge-eating behavior and is worth discussing with a therapist or registered dietitian who specializes in eating concerns. Effective, nonjudgmental treatments are available, and you deserve support rather than stricter rules.

prompt: I don’t love my sister. I would never wish her harm, but if I could, I would wish for us not to be related. Is this cruel? Why must blood mean we have to be friends? Am I being unreasonable and is there a way to fix this? I do care about her, like I do every human being, but I’d rather be with my friends than be with her at all. It’s not just a "teenager phase." I still love my mom and dad, and I’m very close to them. However, it’s my sister I don’t love or have ever really liked at all.
response_text:
Not feeling love or closeness toward your sister doesn’t make you cruel. Family ties can create obligations around basic respect or safety, but they don’t automatically create affection, friendship, or compatibility. You can care about her wellbeing without wanting intimacy or frequent contact, and forcing yourself to perform love may only build resentment.

You don’t necessarily need to “fix” your feelings. Focus instead on how you act: be civil, avoid deliberate harm, and set reasonable boundaries around time together. It may help to reflect on whether there are specific hurts, conflicts, comparisons, or personality differences behind the distance; journaling or talking with a therapist could clarify this. If you want a better relationship, aim for something modest—perhaps respectful coexistence or occasional shared activities—rather than trying to manufacture sibling closeness. If she mistreats you, firmer distance is appropriate; if not, you can still choose your friends as your main emotional family without condemning either of you.

prompt: My mother takes care of niece whom my sister abandoned. She calls me every day complaining, but I don't want to hear it anymore.
response_text:
It makes sense that you feel drained. You can care about your mother and niece without being available for daily venting. Try setting a clear, compassionate boundary: “Mom, I know this is incredibly hard, and I care about you both. I can’t handle daily calls about it. I can listen once a week for 20 minutes, but otherwise I need us to talk about other things.” If she starts complaining outside that time, gently repeat the boundary and end the call.

Encourage her to seek support that doesn’t rely solely on you—trusted relatives, a caregiver or kinship-support group, a therapist, or local social services. If you believe your niece is unsafe or not receiving adequate care, contact the appropriate child-protection or emergency service. Protecting your own emotional capacity is not selfish; consistent limits may preserve your relationship better than growing resentment.

prompt: How do I ever trust another woman? I have found myself constantly reading between the lines with every other woman that I meet. I am having a difficult time making any sort of connection to anyone because of her deception and willingness to say and do literally anything in order to control my emotions. Once the "relationship" was over, she became extremely abusive and has attempted to intimidate me into silence regarding the many false claims made on her immigration application.
response_text:
What you describe sounds like betrayal and emotional abuse, and hypervigilance—reading between every line—can be your nervous system trying to prevent being harmed again. You don’t have to force trust or assume every woman is safe. Start with low-stakes connections, clear boundaries, and let trust build from consistent behavior over time rather than promises. A trauma-informed therapist could help you separate present-day warning signs from fear left by this relationship.

If she is threatening or intimidating you, prioritize safety: limit direct contact, keep communications factual and in writing, preserve messages and dates, and tell trusted people what is happening. Avoid confronting her about immigration claims or making public accusations; consult a qualified attorney or domestic-abuse advocate about safe, lawful options. If threats become immediate or you fear for your safety, contact emergency services or a local abuse hotline. Her actions reflect her choices, not what all women will do.

prompt: Hello, I have a cousin in my family who has been making me feel belittled, insecure, and frustrated during her stay here in the city. I know she comes from a place of love, but she has always been short-fused and highly temperamental if something doesn't work out the way she planned it. I have tried my best to coordinate plans with her, but she always ends up frustrated about the lack of communication I seem to have on my part and then makes condescending comments about my character that include: inconsiderate, negative, oblivious, and self consumed. I have tried to talk to her openly about this, but it always comes back as an attack on my character and I have never heard these comments from anyone else before. I have been thinking a lot about her comments and whether I truly am an inconsiderate person who is not thoughtful, spatially aware of surroundings/people, or positive, but in the end, I am feeling awfully hurt about how this has affected our relationship. What can I do?
response_text:
It makes sense that you feel hurt and unsettled. Her frustration may be real, but broad character judgments and condescending remarks are not constructive feedback—and her intensity does not make those labels accurate. Consider specific behavior separately from insults: if she raises a concrete issue, you can reflect on it or ask a trusted person for an honest perspective, without accepting a global negative view of yourself.

Set a calm, firm boundary: “I’m willing to discuss plans or specific misunderstandings, but I won’t continue conversations where I’m called inconsiderate or self-consumed. If that happens, I’ll step away.” Keep plans simple and confirm details in writing when possible. If she becomes heated, avoid defending your entire character; end the exchange and revisit it only when respectful communication is possible. You may also reduce time together during her stay. Caring about your cousin does not require tolerating repeated belittling, and protecting your emotional well-being is not inconsiderate.

prompt: How do I overcome being jealous of my boyfriends mother?
response_text:
Jealousy toward your boyfriend’s mother can feel embarrassing, but it often points to a deeper need—reassurance, priority, attention, or clearer boundaries—rather than a wish to compete with her. Notice the specific triggers: Does he cancel plans for her, compare you, share private relationship details, or does their closeness simply make you fear being less important? Remind yourself that romantic and parent-child relationships fill different roles; her importance doesn’t automatically reduce yours.

Talk with him when you’re calm, using specific “I” statements rather than criticizing his mother: “I feel pushed aside when our plans change without discussion, and I need us to make decisions together.” Ask for concrete, reasonable changes while respecting their bond. Avoid testing him, demanding he choose, or monitoring their contact, as these usually intensify insecurity. Strengthen your own friendships, interests, and self-worth too. If his relationship with her truly lacks boundaries—or the jealousy remains overwhelming despite reassurance—individual or couples therapy could help clarify healthy expectations.

prompt: I just lost my grandpa and i'm having a rough time with it. I need some help to deal with the loss, but I don’t think I can pay for counseling. Where Can I get help?
response_text:
I’m so sorry about your grandpa. Grief can feel overwhelming, and you don’t have to handle it alone. Free or low-cost help may be available through local hospice programs (often offered even if your grandpa wasn’t their patient), community mental-health clinics, grief-support groups, faith or cultural organizations, and your primary-care clinic. In the U.S., call **211** or visit **211.org** for nearby services; **GriefShare.org**, local hospitals, and the **Open Path Psychotherapy Collective** also list support or reduced-fee counseling. If you’re elsewhere, your country’s health service or a local bereavement charity can direct you.

For now, lean on someone trustworthy, keep basic routines like eating and sleeping, and allow grief to come in waves without judging yourself. If you feel you might harm yourself or cannot stay safe, call emergency services or, in the U.S./Canada, call or text **988** immediately.

prompt: How do I deal with the pain of losing my baby?
response_text:
I’m so sorry. Losing a baby can bring overwhelming grief, shock, anger, guilt, numbness, or even physical pain—there is no “right” way or timeline to grieve, and this was not your fault. For now, focus on getting through the next hour or day: drink water, eat what you can, rest, and let a trusted person stay close or handle practical tasks. You may want to name your baby, keep a memory item, write a letter, or hold a private ritual—only if that feels meaningful.

Please consider support from a grief therapist, your doctor, or a pregnancy/infant-loss group; being with people who understand can lessen the isolation. Partners may grieve differently, so neither person’s response is a measure of love. If the pain feels unbearable, you feel unable to stay safe, or you’re thinking of harming yourself, contact emergency services or a crisis line now (U.S./Canada: call or text 988; elsewhere, use your local crisis service).

prompt: My wife is trying to leave. She agreed to come back and give me a little time. Even said she hopes I can do it. We buried our first born in Jan 13 years ago. She never got past it. So every year around this time, she gets emotional and says she doesn't think she loves me, but then we go back to normal. This time, another guy came in and showed her attention. I'll forgive the cheating if she'll come home.
response_text:
I’m deeply sorry—you’re carrying grief for your child while facing betrayal and the possible end of your marriage. Her anniversary grief may intensify emotions, but it doesn’t automatically explain away years of distress or the cheating. Wanting to forgive is understandable, yet reconciliation requires more than her simply coming home: she must freely choose it, end the other relationship, take responsibility, and help rebuild trust.

Use the time she offered to stay calm rather than persuade, monitor, or pressure her. Tell her you love her, acknowledge both of your grief, and ask whether she is willing to pursue grief-focused individual therapy and couples counseling with a therapist experienced in bereavement and infidelity. Seek your own support now, regardless of her decision, and protect your sleep, eating, finances, and emotional safety. You can offer reconciliation, but you cannot carry it alone or accept an indefinite triangle. If despair becomes unbearable or you might harm yourself or anyone else, contact emergency services or a crisis line immediately.

prompt: How do I cope with losing my mom?
response_text:
I’m so sorry you’re going through this. Losing your mom can feel unreal and overwhelming, and there’s no “right” timeline or way to grieve. Try to focus on getting through one day—or one hour—at a time: eat and rest when you can, let trusted people help, and allow whatever feelings show up without judging them. Small rituals, like writing to her, looking at photos, or doing something she loved, can help you stay connected to her memory.

You don’t have to carry this alone. A grief counselor, support group, faith leader, or trusted friend can offer steady support, especially as others return to their routines. If the pain becomes unbearable or you feel you might hurt yourself, contact emergency services or a crisis line immediately (U.S./Canada: call or text 988; elsewhere, use your local crisis service).

prompt: I loved him more than anything. He passed away on our anniversary which was also the day I was going to apply for our apartment. I'm not handling it well. I moved to a new town and started a new life but nothing helps.
response_text:
I’m so sorry. Losing the person you loved, on a day tied to your anniversary and the future you were building, is an enormous and layered grief. Moving and starting over can’t erase that bond; it makes sense that nothing feels like it helps right now. Try to lower expectations of yourself: focus on getting through one hour or day, eating and sleeping as best you can, and staying connected to someone safe. A grief counselor or bereavement support group may offer steadier support, especially around anniversaries; a small ritual—writing to him, lighting a candle, visiting a meaningful place—can also give the love and pain somewhere to go.

If “not handling it” includes thoughts of hurting yourself or not wanting to live, please don’t stay alone: contact emergency services or a crisis line now (U.S./Canada: call or text 988; elsewhere: findahelpline.com), or go to the nearest emergency department. You deserve support through this, even if relief feels impossible today.

prompt: Can a past therapist disclose information to a current therapist that you are seeing?
response_text:
Yes, sometimes. In the U.S., a former therapist may share relevant information with a current therapist for treatment purposes, depending on HIPAA, state law, agency policies, and any consent/release you signed. Psychotherapy notes usually receive stronger protection and generally require specific authorization. Disclosure may also be allowed or required in emergencies, suspected abuse, or under a valid court order. Providers within the same clinic or health system may have broader access.

You can ask both therapists what information has been or may be shared, request a copy of any release you signed, limit the scope of future disclosures, or revoke authorization going forward. Revocation generally cannot undo information already disclosed. Privacy rules vary by location, so the therapist’s privacy officer or your local licensing board can clarify your rights.

prompt: I terminated my counseling relationship with a social worker several years ago. I am now realizing that I would like to begin counseling again. The social worker’s voicemail message says that he returns calls in 24 hours, but he hasn't called me back. I called him on the weekend and made it clear that I want him to call me back. Can he just ignore me?
response_text:
It’s understandable to feel hurt or anxious when someone you previously trusted doesn’t respond. Since you called on a weekend, “within 24 hours” may mean within one business day, and there could also be illness, vacation, a changed practice, or a voicemail problem. A former therapist generally isn’t obligated to resume treatment, but professional practice would usually involve acknowledging the request or offering referral information when possible.

Wait one or two business days, then leave one brief follow-up with your name, number, and best times to reach you. If there’s still no response, don’t let that delay your care—contact another therapist, your insurer, primary-care clinician, or a local counseling referral service. If you need urgent support or feel unsafe, use a crisis line or emergency service rather than waiting for his call.

prompt: My boyfriend is in the hospital. They won’t tell me what’s wrong and if or when he’s coming back
response_text:
I’m so sorry—this kind of uncertainty can feel frightening and powerless. Hospitals may be legally unable to share information without your boyfriend’s consent, even if you’re his partner. You can ask staff to pass along your name, phone number, and a brief message, and ask whether he can authorize them to update you. If appropriate, contact his designated family member or emergency contact, and ask the hospital’s patient advocate or social worker to explain what information can be shared and how visitation works.

For now, try not to carry this alone: tell someone you trust, eat and rest if you can, and write down questions for when contact becomes possible. If you believe he is in immediate danger or may have disappeared from care, tell hospital staff clearly and contact emergency services.

prompt: What do you do when a therapist and a parent drugs a child and makes up lies in order to stop the other parent's custody visitation?
response_text:
If you believe a child has been drugged or is currently impaired, treat it as an urgent safety issue: seek emergency medical care or call emergency services/poison control, and tell clinicians exactly what you observed. Report the concern to child protective services and law enforcement. Avoid confronting the parent or therapist if that could increase risk, and do not question or coach the child repeatedly—let trained professionals interview them.

Preserve objective evidence: dates, symptoms, messages, medication containers, medical/toxicology records, visitation orders, and the child’s spontaneous words quoted exactly. Contact a family-law attorney promptly about emergency custody or enforcement options, and follow existing court orders unless authorities or the court direct otherwise. You can also file a factual complaint with the therapist’s professional licensing board and employer. Focus on verifiable observations rather than conclusions or accusations; this protects the child and strengthens any investigation.

prompt: I have major depression, severe, PTSD, anxiety disorder, and personality disorder. I had an appointment with my doctor. I was very upset, and I shared with him about that particular drug.
response_text:
It sounds like the appointment was emotionally overwhelming, especially while managing severe depression, PTSD, anxiety, and a personality disorder. Sharing your concerns about a medication was important. If you felt unheard or misunderstood, consider writing down exactly what worries you—such as side effects, dependence, past reactions, or how it affects your symptoms—and contacting your doctor or pharmacist for clarification. Don’t start, stop, or change the dose without medical guidance, since some psychiatric medications require gradual adjustment.

If the drug has caused severe symptoms, you may have taken too much, or you’re thinking about harming yourself, seek urgent help now through emergency services, a crisis line (U.S./Canada: call or text 988), or your nearest emergency department. Stay with a trusted person and move medications or other means of harm out of reach.

prompt: My husband doesn’t trust me for some past we had. I know all marriages have their ups and downs, but sometimes, I feel I am getting tired of the same thing over and over: that I am messing around, which I am not.
response_text:
It sounds exhausting and painful to be repeatedly accused of something you aren’t doing, especially when you’ve tried to move forward from the past. Rebuilding trust can take time, but it cannot depend on endless interrogation, surveillance, or having to prove your innocence over and over. His hurt may be real, yet accusations are not a healthy way to manage it.

Choose a calm moment and say clearly: “I understand the past affected your trust, and I’m willing to work on rebuilding it, but repeated accusations are hurting me and our marriage. We need a different plan.” That plan might include couples counseling, agreed-upon boundaries, and specific behaviors that help rebuild trust without controlling you. If he refuses help, continues accusing you, or becomes threatening or controlling, consider individual counseling and support from someone you trust. You deserve a relationship where concerns can be discussed respectfully and where your emotional safety matters.

prompt: That phrase makes me crazy. It happens anytime I point out something to my husband that he needs to change, such as looking up from his iPad long enough for me to tell him the grandbaby almost pulled the shelf unit over or explaining to him that I got all the things he needs to bake a pie. Another example is when he opens the front door, the dog runs out if he doesn't pick him up. Over and over again, he lets the dog run out, and I am afraid he will get hit by a car.
response_text:
It sounds like his repeated response leaves you feeling dismissed, especially when you’re trying to prevent real dangers. Address this at a calm moment rather than during an incident: “When I raise a safety concern and you say that phrase, I feel ignored and anxious. I need you to acknowledge me and take action, even if you disagree with how I said it.” Try making one brief, concrete request at a time rather than explaining repeatedly.

These examples also call for practical safeguards that don’t depend on either person remembering: anchor the shelf immediately, install a baby gate or barrier near the front door, and agree that the dog is secured before it opens. If he continues minimizing safety concerns or the phrase is part of a broader pattern of contempt or poor communication, couples counseling could help you both feel heard and establish shared responsibilities.

prompt: My husband took a job out of state for the next year and seems to be a different person. Before, he worked and slept, and on off days, he'd stay home because he didn't want to do anything else. Now he's going out with friends several nights a week while I'm still home working a 50 hours a week job and taking care of two kids by myself. He's suddenly saying he misses me and wants me to be his adored wife, but the whole time, I'm remembering how I've been emotionally starving for the last five years.
response_text:
Your resentment and confusion make sense. His new attention may feel painful rather than reassuring because it highlights what you asked for—and didn’t receive—for years, while you’re now carrying work, parenting, and the household alone. You don’t have to become an “adored wife” on demand or ignore the emotional neglect you’ve experienced.

Tell him plainly that words aren’t enough; rebuilding closeness requires consistent action and accountability. Ask for specific changes, such as taking on parenting and household responsibilities from afar, protecting regular time for meaningful connection, and discussing why he had so little energy for your relationship but now has energy for friends. Couples counseling, including telehealth, could help you address the past five years rather than covering them with affection. Pay attention to whether he listens without defensiveness and follows through over time. You’re allowed to move slowly, set boundaries, and decide what you need before offering renewed intimacy.

prompt: My husband and I have been together since high school. We have been married going on for nearly ten years, and we have three beautiful children. A few weeks ago, my husband decided he need some time apart and moved over to his dad’s for a while. He comes home to see the kids and acts like there is not too much wrong. Can this marriage be saved or is it too late? He said he would go to counseling, so I don't think he has given up.
response_text:
It may not be too late. His willingness to attend counseling suggests there is still some openness, but saving the marriage will require honest communication and effort from both of you. A temporary separation can sometimes create space to understand what is wrong, though uncertainty can feel very painful.

Ask him for a calm, direct conversation about what “time apart” means: what he needs, whether you are both committed to trying, expectations around contact and fidelity, parenting arrangements, and when you will reassess. Schedule couples counseling soon rather than leaving it vague; individual counseling could also help you cope and clarify your own needs. Keep the children’s routines stable and avoid involving them in adult conflict. Most importantly, pay attention to consistent actions—not just reassurance—and remember that you deserve clarity, respect, and support regardless of the outcome.

prompt: I have been with my husband for almost 7 years. We got engaged a little after 5 years of being together. I had always been clear that I wanted to get married and I sadly would drop hints about how i wanted him to propose. When he did propose it was during a random vacation that I had planned. I was happy but I couldn't help feeling disappointed too. I had told him numerous times before that I wanted him to do it in front of my friends and family. I know it sounds dumb to be upset but I couldn't help how I was feeling. We are now married but the wedding and ring were also far from what I wanted and it wasn't due to lack of funds. I know this is all material and the marriage is the most important thing but I cant help but get jealous and envious every time I see someone get a proposal or wedding that I had wanted. I cant help my anger because I know we only get one proposal and one wedding. What I wanted will never happen. I have been working on my feelings for the past year and half to get over it. I try to focus on our marriage but every time I see someone have the best proposals and weddings I get upset. I know it is selfish and I know its petty but I just can't control it. It's ruining our relationship because I constantly think about it. Plus, I get mad at him for small things because I am trying to hide the fact that I am so disappointed. Why can't I move on?
response_text:
You may not be grieving the ring or wedding so much as the feeling that your clearly expressed wishes weren’t heard, valued, or acted on. That can leave a lasting wound: “Did he know me, and did what mattered to me matter to him?” Jealousy then reactivates that hurt. This doesn’t make you selfish or petty, but hiding it and expressing it through anger over small things will keep the resentment alive.

Have an honest, calm conversation focused on the meaning rather than blaming his choices: “I love our marriage, but I’m still hurt because I felt unseen during those milestones. I need understanding and repair, not an argument about whether I should care.” Consider creating a meaningful new ritual together—an anniversary celebration, vow renewal, special photos, or a ring chosen jointly—not to erase the past, but to build a memory where you feel considered. If conversations become defensive or repetitive, couples therapy could help you process the disappointment and identify whether feeling unheard is a broader pattern.

prompt: When my daughter is stressed about a silly thing from school, she starts crying and freaking out. She is a bright student, always has a 4.0, but I am afraid she is stressing too much. I’m afraid it’s going to break her. I don't know if I should get her to a doctor or someone because this is not normal.
response_text:
It makes sense to be concerned. Even if the school issue seems small to you, her distress is real; high-achieving students can feel intense pressure, perfectionism, or anxiety. In calm moments, avoid calling it “silly” and try: “I can see this feels overwhelming. Do you want me to listen, help problem-solve, or just stay with you?” During an episode, focus on slow breathing, a quiet space, and reassurance rather than grades or solutions.

Consider scheduling a routine visit with her pediatrician, especially if this happens often, is worsening, or affects sleep, eating, friendships, school attendance, or enjoyment. They can screen for anxiety and refer her to a child/adolescent therapist; seeking support early does not mean anything is “wrong” with her. You might also discreetly check with her school counselor about stressors or bullying. If she talks about self-harm, not wanting to live, or cannot stay safe, seek emergency help immediately.

prompt: My ex-wife married and used me to have a child. She now uses that child as a pawn. I know my child misses me, but I need to move on and not live in the past. How do I do this? Do I see my child as much as possible or very little? Is it more confusing for the child?
response_text:
I’m sorry—this sounds deeply painful. Moving on from the marriage does not require moving away from your child. In general, children do best with safe, predictable, consistent contact with both parents; sporadic or very limited visits can be more confusing than a dependable routine. Aim for as much regular involvement as is healthy and permitted, rather than contact driven by conflict or emotion. Reassure your child that the separation is not their fault, avoid criticizing their mother in front of them, and focus on being calm, reliable, and present.

Keep communication with your ex brief, factual, and child-focused, preferably in writing. Follow any custody agreement and document missed or obstructed contact without involving your child. A family-law professional or mediator can help protect parenting time, while an individual therapist can help you grieve the relationship and separate those feelings from fatherhood. If contact is unsafe for you or the child, seek professional and legal guidance about supervised or modified arrangements.

prompt: Can a counselor take sides with one parent and allow a parent to order the child to tell the counselor "every detail" about what happened during the other parent’s visitation in order to help build a case for child custody?
response_text:
A counselor generally should not “take sides” or use therapy to gather evidence for one parent’s custody case. Their role is usually to support the child’s wellbeing, remain clinically neutral, and avoid pressuring or coaching the child. Asking a child to recount “every detail” of the other parent’s visitation can be distressing, create loyalty conflicts, and contaminate information—especially if abuse allegations may require a trained forensic interview. However, counselors must report reasonable suspicions of abuse or imminent danger, and confidentiality for minors varies by jurisdiction, court orders, and custody arrangements.

Ask the counselor, in writing, to clarify their role, who consented to treatment, what information is shared with each parent, and whether records may be used in court. Document concerning requests without interrogating the child yourself. If this appears improper, consult a family-law attorney, guardian ad litem/custody evaluator, the counselor’s clinical supervisor, or their licensing board. If the child reports abuse or is in immediate danger, contact child protective services or emergency services.

prompt: I have four children. One of them is in her 20s, and she cannot afford to go, nor can I pay for her. She went last year for two weeks by herself.
response_text:
It sounds painful to want to include all four children while facing financial limits, especially when your daughter may feel left out. Her having gone alone last year may be relevant, but it doesn’t necessarily erase either her disappointment or your guilt. You’re not failing her by being unable to pay.

Try speaking with her directly and compassionately: explain the financial reality without over-defending it, acknowledge that missing out may hurt, and reassure her that she matters. If appropriate, you could explore a shorter or less expensive option, shared costs, or meaningful time together before or after. You can care about her feelings while still holding a firm financial boundary.

prompt: I am divorced and happily remarried. Our blended family of children are in their 20s. My youngest, age 20, continues to call me crazy and favors her dad. He was abusive to me, and I left with injuries. He never wanted kids, and I did. He paid child support only through forced wage earners. Now my daughters favor him after all the sacrifices I made for them the past 15 years as a single mom. I don’t deny them a relationship with their dad, but to be called crazy and then watch them hang out with him hurts me to the very core. I’m not sure how to handle this.
response_text:
What you’re feeling makes sense: being called “crazy” and seeing your daughters embrace someone who harmed you can feel like betrayal and erasure of everything you endured. Their relationship with their father, however, does not necessarily mean they disbelieve you or value your sacrifices less; adult children often cope with divided loyalties by simplifying or avoiding painful family history.

You can protect yourself without asking them to choose sides. Calmly say, “You’re free to have a relationship with Dad, but calling me crazy is disrespectful. If it happens, I’ll end the conversation or visit.” Avoid arguing about who was the better parent or trying to prove the abuse; share your experience once, factually, if appropriate, and then let their views be theirs. Focus on building relationships with them in the present, while grieving the recognition you hoped to receive. A trauma-informed therapist or domestic-abuse survivor group could help you process this pain and hold firm boundaries without being pulled back into the old conflict.

prompt: How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?
response_text:
Counseling usually ends when the client’s goals have been met, symptoms are manageable, and the client can use coping skills and supports independently. A counselor may also recommend ending or changing treatment if progress has stalled, a different specialty or level of care is needed, the counselor is leaving the practice, or practical issues make continued work impossible. Clients can also choose to stop at any time.

Ethically, termination should generally be discussed collaboratively rather than happening suddenly. The counselor should explain the reason, review progress and remaining needs, create a relapse-prevention or follow-up plan, and provide referrals when appropriate. Immediate termination is uncommon but may occur because of serious boundary violations, threats, repeated nonattendance or nonpayment, or other safety/legal concerns; even then, counselors should avoid abandonment and offer reasonable transition support when possible. If termination feels abrupt or confusing, you can ask for the rationale, a final session, records, and referrals.

prompt: My therapist is gay so there are no sexual issues here. However, my therapist for six years has made me believe that he cares about me and that we are friends. I have loaned money to him many times, and he always paid me back. I had a medical emergency last weekend and I was heavily medicated. I knew that this therapist came into my home and wrote down my credit card information so he could pay back what he owed me, but this therapist dropped me off and never came again. I don't know what to do.
response_text:
I’m sorry—this sounds frightening and like a serious breach of professional boundaries. A therapist should not borrow money from a client, enter the client’s home while they are heavily medicated, or access credit-card information. His sexual orientation doesn’t determine whether exploitation or other boundary violations occurred.

Contact your card issuer/bank immediately: freeze or replace the card, change related passwords/PINs, review transactions, and dispute anything unauthorized. Write down what happened while it is fresh, save messages and loan/payment records, and ask a trusted person to help you. If property or money was taken, consider contacting police or a local legal-aid service. Report the therapist to his licensing board and, if applicable, his clinic/employer; you can search your state/province’s professional licensing website. Do not meet him alone or lend more money. Arrange care with a different licensed therapist or your doctor, especially after the medical emergency. If you feel unsafe or medically unwell, contact emergency services now.

prompt: I just wanted to get to know one so I can hear about their college experience and the courses they took. I also wanted to know if they enjoy their job and how long they were in school.
response_text:
It sounds like you’re looking for an informational interview with someone in that profession—not asking for a major commitment. That’s a reasonable way to learn whether the career might suit you.

You could contact professionals through your college’s alumni network, career center, LinkedIn, or a relevant professional association. Try: “Hi, I’m exploring a career in your field and would appreciate 15–20 minutes to hear about your college experience, coursework, length of training, and what you enjoy or find challenging about your job.
